paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A bright red cardinal crooning loudly from the treetops is a sure sign that spring has arrived in North America. But the bird is also displaying a highly unusual talent. Songbirds like cardinals are among the few creatures that actually learn the vocalizations they make. Among the others, two groups are also birds — hummingbirds and parrots — and the rest are mammals: bats, cetaceans (whales and dolphins), elephants and humans. All other creatures produce sounds that, according to current research, are programmed by the species’ genes. ‘Not even the chimpanzee, our closest living relative, is a vocal learner,’ says Erich Jarvis, a neurobiologist at Duke University Medical Center.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: According to Jarvis and other scientists, baby songbirds begin to sing much like human infants begin to speak. Both start by listening to their parents or other adults and memorizing the sounds. They then mimic their mentors, slowly perfecting their ‘language’ over time through practice. Like humans, young birds take bits and pieces of the sounds adults produce, repeating them in completely random sequences until the proper vocalization takes shape. For songbirds, the final phase often takes place once a fledgling leaves its parents’ territory. After settling in a new location, the bird may incorporate into its own repertoire local ‘dialects’ of the species’ song. Biologists have discovered that North American chickadees on the island of Martha’s Vineyard, for example, have different dialects from chickadees in the rest of Massachusetts. Like most people, who after adolescence have difficulty learning a foreign language, most songbirds lose the ability to learn new melodies after they reach maturity. A handful of species, however — including mynas, starlings and mockingbirds — are able to pick up new tunes throughout their lives.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A few years ago, Jarvis and his colleagues observed that when a songbird, parrot or hummingbird is producing its learned vocalization, a similar set of structures in the birds’ brains becomes active. The finding was surprising because the three avian groups are only distantly related to one another. At the same time, they are closely related to other birds that are not vocal learners. Flycatchers, for example, belong to the same order as songbirds — Passeriformes — yet no flycatcher species tested so far displays the vocal learning trait.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One possible explanation, says Jarvis, is that vocal learning birds have a common ancestor that possessed the skill. Another hypothesis is that vocal learners evolved similar brain structures independently, just as birds and bats separately evolved wings that turned out to be so much alike. Discoveries about the human brain lend weight to this latter hypothesis. Scientists conducting imaging studies have found that when people speak, parts of their brains that are similar to those of vocalizing songbirds, parrots and hummingbirds become active. However vocal learning evolved, Jarvis and other scientists say that a better understanding of how birds learn to sing should provide insight into human language acquisition, as well as potential innovative treatments for speech disorders. ‘The clinical implications are significant,’ he says.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Biologists have proposed at least two reasons why vocal learning would be favored during a species’ evolution. One advantage is that the trait provides flexibility to animals that must communicate across a variety of habitat types. While vocal-nonlearning doves don’t need to adjust their simple, low-frequency calls that travel so well along the ground — nor flycatchers their high-pitched songs that pass best through the air — most songbirds move in and out and throughout the layers of a forest, requiring a larger repertoire of sounds.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: But an even stronger selection pressure for vocal learning, say biologists, is mate attraction. Scientists studying several songbird species have demonstrated that females prefer males that produce the most complex songs. And Cornell University psychologist and neurobiologist Timothy DeVoogd discovered that a male’s superior singing skills correlate with larger brain structures — and that among zebra finches, these are inherited by the birds’ sons. ‘If you’re picking a male with a fancier song,’ says DeVoogd, ‘you’re probably also picking one who’s a little bit smarter.’ What’s more, in a study involving song sparrows, Duke University biologist Stephen Nowicki found that birds with inferior songs had suffered stress early in life, which he suggests may have hampered brain development.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Given such clear advantages, why is it that so few animal species are vocal learners? To most biologists, the answer remains a fascinating mystery. Jarvis, however, has his own idea. Like a peacock’s elaborate tail, complex vocalizations may entice females, he suggests, but predators notice them too. Following that logic, the cardinal singing boldly from a treetop may indeed make a worthy mate. After all, says Jarvis, the better you sing your song, the more attention you’ll get. And if you can do that and also escape all the predators that want to catch you, you must be a pretty good animal.
